questions.prompt: An instance has a Change Request approval process that was built years ago in the legacy Workflow Editor, and it still runs correctly today. Per this course, what should you do with it?
options: Leave it running as-is -- ServiceNow doesn't force existing Workflow Editor automation onto Flow Designer, so unless it's actually broken there's no reason to rebuild it
Rebuild it in Flow Designer immediately, because the Workflow Editor is deprecated and no longer executes
Delete it, since `wf_workflow` records can't coexist with `sys_hub_flow` records in the same instance
Convert it automatically using Flow Designer's built-in Workflow import wizard
questions.explain: Lesson 1 is explicit: ServiceNow has not removed the Workflow Editor and does not force a migration, because that risks breaking production automation. Both tools coexist -- legacy Workflows keep running as built, while Flow Designer is for new automation going forward.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: every Flow Designer flow, under the hood, is a record on the ________ table.
questions.explain: Lesson 2 establishes that every Flow -- and every Subflow -- is structurally a record on sys_hub_flow, one Trigger followed by an ordered sequence of Actions.

questions.prompt: Match each Flow Designer building block to what it actually is.
right: Fires on a time-based schedule rather than reacting to a record change
A single reusable, configurable step such as Create Record or Send Notification
A sys_hub_flow record flagged as callable by other flows, with no trigger of its own
Fires when a record on a chosen table is created, updated, or deleted, narrowed by a condition
questions.explain: Lessons 2 and 3 define each term precisely: an Action is one configurable step; a Subflow is a sys_hub_flow record built to be called, not triggered; a Record trigger reacts to a record change narrowed by a condition; a Scheduled trigger fires on a timer.

questions.prompt: A Record trigger is set to fire on the Incident table for "Created" with no condition at all. What actually happens?
options: The flow fires on every single new Incident, regardless of priority, category, or any other field
The flow never fires, because a Record trigger requires at least one condition to be valid
The flow fires only on the first Incident created each day
ServiceNow automatically applies a default condition of Priority is Critical
questions.explain: Lesson 3 states directly that without a condition, a Record trigger set to Created on Incident fires on every single new Incident -- the condition is what narrows it down to only the records that should actually fire it.

questions.prompt: Put these steps from Lesson 4's worked scenario (notify a manager when a Priority 1 Incident is created) in the order they actually happen.
items: A Record trigger is configured on the Incident table for 'Created', with a condition of Priority is 1 - Critical
A Notify action is added, addressed using a data pill that resolves to the assignment group's manager
The flow is saved, which preserves the configuration but does not yet run it against real records
The flow is activated, so the trigger engine begins watching for matching Incidents
questions.explain: Lesson 4 walks this exact order: build the narrowed trigger, add the Notify action with a dynamic recipient, save (inert), then activate -- the deliberate step that turns the trigger engine on.

questions.prompt: In Flow Designer, what is a data pill?
options: A draggable token representing a specific piece of output from the trigger or an earlier step, referenced instead of being typed in by hand
A value you type directly into a field, independent of any trigger or step output
A scheduled job that runs a flow repeatedly at a fixed interval
A warning icon shown when a required field is left empty
A custom table used to store flow execution history
A permission that controls who can activate a flow
questions.explain: Lesson 5 defines a data pill as a draggable token representing output from the trigger or a prior step -- it always comes from somewhere upstream, which is what distinguishes it from a flow variable.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a flow variable, not a data pill -- a flow variable is explicitly defined by the builder ahead of time and doesn't come from the trigger or any step's output, which is exactly the opposite of what makes something a data pill.

questions.prompt: Select every statement that correctly distinguishes a flow variable from a data pill, per Lesson 5.
options: A data pill's value always comes from somewhere upstream -- the trigger or a prior step's output
A flow variable is explicitly defined by the builder, independent of any trigger or step output
A flow variable can automatically hold today's incoming record's Priority field with no extra steps
Both a flow variable and a data pill are referenced the same drag-and-drop way once defined
A data pill must always be a numeric value
questions.explain: A data pill's value always traces back to the trigger or a prior action's output; a flow variable is defined explicitly by the builder with no natural upstream source; both are then referenced the same drag-and-drop way. A flow variable has no automatic connection to incoming record data, and pills aren't restricted to numbers.

questions.prompt: A flow's If/Else condition checks "Cost is greater than 1000." A Requested Item costs exactly $1,000. Which branch runs?
options: The Else branch, because $1,000 is not strictly greater than 1000 under that operator
The If branch, because $1,000 is close enough to the threshold to count
Neither branch runs, and the flow stalls indefinitely
Both branches run simultaneously and then reconverge
questions.explain: Lesson 6's own check-yourself scenario makes this exact point: the operator chosen for the condition matters precisely because 'greater than' excludes a value equal to the threshold -- a $1,000 item evaluates false and takes the Else branch.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Request has four approved Requested Items, and a For Each loop contains a single Create Record action inside its loop body. The flow ends up creating ________ fulfillment task records.
questions.explain: Lesson 7 is explicit that everything inside a For Each's loop body runs once per item -- four items in the list means the loop body, and its Create Record action, runs four separate times.

questions.prompt: In Lesson 8's Equipment Request lab, a Request has two Requested Items: a $2,000 laptop and a $50 cable. Per the designed flow (For Each over the items, an If/Else inside checking price against the extra_approval_threshold flow variable, then a Create Record per item), what is the outcome?
options: The loop runs twice; the If branch fires once (for the laptop) and the Else branch fires once (for the cable); two fulfillment tasks exist at the end
The loop runs once total, covering both items in a single pass
The If branch fires for both items because the Request itself was already approved
No fulfillment tasks are created until both items individually pass a second approval
questions.explain: The For Each iterates once per Requested Item (two passes). The If/Else inside evaluates the current item's price against the threshold on each pass independently -- true for the $2,000 laptop, false for the $50 cable. The Create Record step, placed inside the loop, still runs once per item regardless of which branch it took, producing two tasks total.

questions.prompt: A flow needs to change a value on the Incident record that triggered it. Which built-in action should it use?
options: Update Record, because the trigger record already exists and only needs to be modified
Create Record, because every action in a flow should produce a new row
Notify, because sending a message is the only way to change a field
Ask for Approval, since any field change technically requires sign-off first
questions.explain: Lesson 9 draws this distinction directly: Create Record always produces a brand-new record, while Update Record modifies a record that already exists -- most often the trigger record itself, which is automatically available as a data pill.

questions.prompt: Match each approval scenario to the correct Ask for Approval variant from Lesson 10.
left: A single named manager must sign off on a new hire's equipment request
Any one of three regional directors responding first settles the decision
Every member of a multi-person change advisory board must sign off before implementation
The flow pauses and creates real approval records for a human to act on
right: sysapproval_approver records are generated and the flow genuinely pauses until they resolve
questions.explain: Lesson 10 lays out all three variants and confirms that any approval action creates real sysapproval_approver records and genuinely pauses flow execution until a final state is reached -- it isn't a cosmetic delay.

questions.prompt: Three different flows in an instance each need to calculate an SLA due date from a priority level. Per Lesson 11, what's the real cost of copy-pasting that calculation logic into all three flows instead of building one custom Action Designer action?
options: If the business rule behind the calculation ever changes, someone has to find and correctly update it in all three places, and missing one silently leaves that flow out of sync with the others
Nothing changes functionally -- copy-pasting logic into multiple flows and centralizing it in one action produce identical long-term maintenance cost
Flow Designer technically refuses to save more than one flow containing the same calculation
Copy-pasting the logic makes each individual flow run measurably slower at execution time
questions.explain: Lesson 11 is direct about this: centralizing logic in one custom action means fixing it once benefits every caller automatically, while copy-pasted logic has to be found and correctly re-edited everywhere it was duplicated -- and missing one copy is exactly how flows drift out of sync.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the tool used to build a custom, reusable Flow Designer action -- defining its Inputs, internal steps, and Outputs -- is called ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 11 names Action Designer as the tool for building a custom action once, so every flow that needs that logic calls the same action instead of re-implementing it.

questions.prompt: In the Lesson 12 New Hire Equipment Request lab, why is Step 2 (resolving the manager and running a single-approver approval) a strong candidate for a custom reusable action, while Step 1 (Create Record opening the Asset Request) is not?
options: Every onboarding flow in the organization needs the exact same manager-approval pattern, while the Create Record step is specific enough to this one request type that extracting it wouldn't save much
Create Record actions can never be reused across flows under any circumstances
Approval actions are technically incapable of running inline inside a flow without Action Designer
Step 1 already runs inside a subflow, so it doesn't need to be a custom action
questions.explain: Lesson 12's own closing analysis makes this exact comparison: the manager-approval pattern repeats identically across equipment, access, and office-space onboarding flows, which is the textbook reuse case, while the asset-record creation is specific enough to this one request that duplicating it elsewhere wouldn't save much.

questions.prompt: What is the real, decisive test for choosing to build a Subflow instead of a top-level Flow?
options: Whether the same sequence of steps needs to run from more than one place, versus reacting directly to a record event or schedule that only a Flow's trigger can provide
Whether the logic involves an approval action anywhere in its steps
Whether the flow needs to call a REST API at some point
Whether the flow was built by an administrator versus a developer
questions.explain: Lesson 13 states the test directly: build a top-level Flow when logic needs to react directly to a record event or schedule (only a Flow has a Trigger); build a Subflow when the same sequence of steps needs to run from more than one place.

questions.prompt: A single sequence of steps (notify and log a decision) will only ever be used by one flow in the instance, with no other caller in sight. Per Lesson 13, should it be built as a subflow anyway, 'just in case'?
options: No -- wrapping it in a subflow with no actual reuse adds an extra layer of indirection for no real benefit; a Subflow earns its place only once there's real or clearly foreseeable reuse
Yes -- every flow's logic should always be built as a subflow regardless of how many callers it has
Yes, but only if the flow also contains an If/Else branch
No -- Flow Designer technically prevents a subflow from having only one caller
questions.explain: Lesson 13 directly answers this: subflows aren't automatically 'more correct' -- a top-level Flow is still right when nothing else in the instance needs that same sequence, and building a subflow without real reuse just adds indirection with no benefit.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about a Subflow's Inputs and Outputs, per Lesson 14.
options: Inputs are a named, typed list defining exactly what the subflow needs from whatever calls it, because a subflow has no trigger handing it data automatically
Outputs become available as data pills to the steps that run after the Call Subflow action in the calling flow
A subflow's Inputs and Outputs are defined by writing an actual function signature in JavaScript
Without defined Outputs, the subflow's internal work would be invisible to whatever called it
questions.explain: Lesson 14 explains that Inputs exist because a subflow has no trigger to hand it data automatically, Outputs surface as data pills after the Call Subflow action, and undefined outputs would leave the subflow's work invisible to its caller. It explicitly notes the authoring experience is configuration-based, not writing a real code function signature.

questions.prompt: Put these steps from the Lesson 15 subflow extraction lab in the order they're actually performed.
items: Compare the duplicated block across all three flows to confirm the steps are identical and only the data (record and message wording) varies
Design the new subflow's Inputs (Manager, Request Record, Message) and Outputs (Decision, Decision Date)
Build the subflow once, named 'Notify and Log Manager Decision', with those Inputs and Outputs defined
Replace the duplicated inline block in each of the three calling flows with a single Call Subflow action
Run each flow against a test record to verify behavior is unchanged after the refactor
questions.explain: Lesson 15 walks exactly this order: confirm the logic is truly identical before extracting it, design the Inputs/Outputs from what the three flows actually needed, build the subflow once, swap each flow's inline block for a Call Subflow action, then verify nothing changed in behavior.

questions.prompt: A flow's Service Catalog trigger is set to fire on 'Requested Item Created' but is accidentally left without a cat_item filter. What actually goes wrong?
options: The flow fires for every catalog item requested anywhere in the system, not just the one it was built for
The flow never fires at all, because a Service Catalog trigger requires a cat_item filter to be valid
The flow fires once per Request record regardless of how many items it contains
The trigger silently defaults to the most recently created catalog item
questions.explain: Lesson 16's own check-yourself scenario is this exact question: without the cat_item filter narrowing the trigger to one specific catalog item, every catalog request on every item in the system would fire that same flow.

questions.prompt: Why does a Service Catalog trigger fire on the Requested Item (sc_req_item) rather than the parent Request (sc_request)?
options: A single Request can contain multiple Requested Items, and triggering on the Requested Item gives each item its own flow execution, scoped to its own variables, independent of other items in the same cart
The Request record doesn't technically exist until after the Requested Item is created
sc_request has no reference field pointing back to the catalog item ordered
Variable values are only ever stored on the Request, never on the Requested Item
questions.explain: Lesson 16 explains that triggering on the Request would fire one execution covering every item in a multi-item cart with no clean way to isolate each item's fulfillment logic -- triggering on the Requested Item avoids that entirely.

questions.prompt: A request needs sign-off from any one of three regional directors, and the business wants whichever director responds first to settle the decision immediately. Per Lesson 17, what happens if this is misconfigured as an 'all' approval instead of 'any'?
options: The stage would wait for every one of the three directors to respond before resolving, even though the business only wanted the first response to count
Nothing would change -- 'any' and 'all' behave identically when there are exactly three approvers
The flow would fail outright with a configuration error at save time
The approval would resolve immediately regardless of the setting, since directors are a privileged role
questions.explain: Lesson 17 defines 'any' as resolving on the first response received and 'all' as waiting for every named approver -- configuring this stage as 'all' when the business wanted the first response to settle it would force an unwanted wait on the other two directors.

questions.prompt: In Lesson 18's New Software License Request lab, a license costs exactly $500. Per the stated business rule (under $500 needs only Manager approval; $500 or more needs Manager approval then Finance approval), fill in the blank: this license requires ________ approval stage(s).
questions.explain: The If/Else compares License Cost against 500 using 'is less than'. $500 is not less than 500, so it falls into the Else branch requiring Manager approval followed by Finance approval -- two stages, not one.

questions.prompt: What is IntegrationHub, as introduced in this course?
options: ServiceNow's integration add-on, often separately licensed, that adds spokes and a generic REST step to Flow Designer so flows can reach external systems through configuration instead of code
A built-in, always-on feature of every ServiceNow instance for managing internal record relationships
A scripting language used exclusively inside Business Rules
A reporting dashboard that visualizes flow execution history
A table that stores every REST API ever called by the instance
A replacement for the entire Service Catalog module
questions.explain: Lesson 19 describes IntegrationHub as ServiceNow's integration add-on, frequently a separately licensed capability, that lets a flow reach outside ServiceNow using configuration (spokes, the generic REST step) instead of custom code.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is wrong because Lesson 19 explicitly compares IntegrationHub to Performance Analytics as 'often a separately licensed capability layered on top of the base platform -- not something every instance has turned on by default,' the opposite of an always-on built-in feature.

questions.prompt: A flow needs to call an external CRM system's REST API, and no pre-built spoke exists for that CRM. Per Lessons 19-20, what should the REST step reference for its endpoint and authentication, instead of a hardcoded URL and credential?
options: A Connection & Credential Alias, a reusable record that stores the connection details centrally so every flow using it picks up a credential rotation automatically
A Script Include containing the raw HTTP request logic
A flow variable typed as 'Reference' pointing at the sys_user table
The REST step cannot be configured without a pre-built spoke, so a Script step is the only option
questions.explain: Lesson 20 explains that hardcoding a URL and credential works only until the credential rotates or a second flow needs the same system -- the Connection & Credential Alias stores those details once, centrally, so every referencing flow picks up a rotation automatically.

questions.prompt: Put these steps from the Lesson 21 IntegrationHub lab in the order the finished flow actually executes them.
items: A Record trigger fires on Incident created with a condition of Priority is 1 - Critical
The Teams Spoke's 'Post Message' action posts an alert to the on-call channel using data pills from the trigger
A generic REST step performs a GET against the CRM via a Connection & Credential Alias, mapping the account_tier field from the response into a data pill
An Update Record action writes the account_tier data pill back onto the originating incident
questions.explain: Lesson 21 lays the finished flow out top to bottom exactly this way: trigger, then the Teams Spoke action (configuration only, no REST needed), then the generic REST step for the CRM lookup (no spoke exists for it), then the Update Record action writing the mapped value back onto the incident.

questions.prompt: A flow 'hasn't produced its expected result yet.' Per Lesson 22, how do you tell, from the execution log alone, whether it's actually broken versus simply paused?
options: A paused run shows the flow sitting at a specific action with a status like 'waiting' and no error; a failed run shows a specific action with an error status and an error message describing what went wrong
A paused run and a failed run are indistinguishable in the execution log -- you have to re-read the flow's logic to tell them apart
Only failed runs appear in the execution log at all; paused runs are invisible until they resolve
A paused run always resolves itself automatically within 24 hours, so no action is needed either way
questions.explain: Lesson 22 draws this distinction directly: paused shows 'waiting' with no error (legitimately waiting on something external, like an unanswered approval), while failed shows an error status and message -- treating one as the other is called the most common troubleshooting mistake the log exists to prevent.

questions.prompt: Select every recurring flow failure category described in Lesson 23.
options: A data pill silently resolving to null because the field or related record it references no longer matches what the flow expects at the point the step runs
A required action input left unmapped, causing that step to fail outright with an error naming the specific missing input
A data type mismatch in an If/Else condition quietly sending the flow down the unexpected branch instead of throwing an error
An approval routed to the wrong person or an empty group, leaving the flow waiting indefinitely with nothing actually broken in the flow's own logic
Flow Designer automatically retrying a flow up to five times before marking it permanently failed
questions.explain: Lesson 23 names exactly these as the recurring failure categories: null/empty pills, an unmapped required input, a data type mismatch in a condition, and an approval stuck on a wrong or empty recipient -- plus IntegrationHub REST failures. There's no automatic five-retry mechanism described anywhere in the lesson.

questions.prompt: In Lesson 24's 'stuck' New Hire Onboarding scenario, the execution log shows the run waiting at a Manager Approval step, and the resolved approver pill is empty because Maria Chen's manager field was never populated. What was the actual defect, and what two-part fix does the lesson recommend?
options: The defect was upstream data quality, not the flow's logic; the fix is to correct Maria's manager field immediately (unblocking her today) and add a fallback-approver check to the flow itself (so a future hire with the same gap doesn't silently stall)
The defect was a bug in the Approval action itself; the fix is to rebuild the entire approval step from scratch
The defect was that Record triggers can't reliably fire on User record creation; the fix is to switch the trigger to Scheduled
The defect was a missing Connection & Credential Alias; the fix is to create one and point the Approval action at it
questions.explain: Lesson 24 is explicit that the flow performed correctly -- it's a data quality gap upstream, not a flow logic bug. The real fix has two parts: the immediate, non-technical fix (populate the manager field and restart the approval) and the durable fix (add a check that routes to a fallback approver when the manager field is blank).

questions.prompt: In the capstone's Contractor Offboarding flow, why does Lesson 25 choose a Scheduled trigger over a Record trigger, even though the end_date field lives directly on the contractor record?
options: The end_date field was set weeks earlier at onboarding time and nothing changes on the record the day it actually matters, so there's no record-change event for a Record trigger to react to -- the process depends on time passing, which only a Scheduled trigger's daily query can detect
Record triggers technically cannot be configured on a custom table that extends sys_user
A Scheduled trigger is always the safer default choice regardless of what the business process actually needs
Flow Designer requires every capstone-level flow to use a Scheduled trigger for grading purposes
questions.explain: Lesson 25 makes this exact distinction: a Record trigger is built for events -- something changing right now -- but nothing changes on the contractor record the day the end_date arrives, since it was set weeks earlier. A Scheduled trigger's daily query is what actually detects that a relevant date has arrived.
